chunks: "A reset signal forces the processor and its peripherals into a known initial state and then lets it start executing from a defined address.
Without it, flip-flops come up in random states when power is applied, and the CPU could start running garbage.

What happens: while reset is asserted, the core is halted, registers return to default values, peripherals are disabled, GPIO pins go to a safe state, usually inputs, and clocks fall back to the default internal oscillator.
When reset is released, a Cortex-M loads the stack pointer and the reset vector from the start of the vector table and begins running my startup code.
Reset comes from several sources. Power-on reset holds the chip until the supply is above a threshold.
Brown-out reset triggers if the supply sags below it, so the chip doesn't run, or worse corrupt flash, on a bad voltage.
There's the external reset pin, usually active low, tied to a pull-up, a button and maybe a supervisor chip or debugger.
The watchdog resets it if the firmware hangs, and software can trigger a reset on purpose.
It's useful because it gives deterministic start-up, a way to recover from a lock-up, and protection from running outside the valid supply range.
And I'd read the reset-cause flag at boot to know why it restarted."
